items.title: Transformation's Remaining Faults, and the Real Cost of Simply Obtaining Food

items.zh: 由是日日數應洗淨。或手、或足、或餘支節誤觸著時，若自若他皆生厭惡。又由此緣，發生身中多種疾病。所謂癰痤、乾癬、濕癬、疥癩、疽疔、上氣、疨瘶、皰漿、噦噎、乾消、癲癎、寒熱、黃病、熱血、陰㾽。如是等類無量疾病，由飲食故，身中生起。或由所食不平和故，於其身中不消而住。是名飲食變異種類所有過患。云何追求種類過患？謂於飲食追求種類有多過患。或有積集所作過患、或有防護所作過患、或壞親愛所作過患、或無厭足所作過患、或不自在所作過患、或有惡行所作過患。云何名為於食積集所作過患？謂如有一，為食因緣，寒時為寒之所逼惱，熱時為熱之所逼惱，種種策勵劬勞勤苦。營農、牧牛、商估、計算、書數、雕印，及餘種種工巧業處，為得未得所有飲食，或為積聚。如為飲食，為飲食緣，當知亦爾。如是策勵劬勞勤苦，方求之時，所作事業若不諧遂；由是因緣，愁憂燋惱、拊胸傷歎、悲泣迷悶，何乃我功唐捐無果？如是名為於食積集所作過患。云何名為於食防護所作過患？謂所作業若得諧遂，為護因緣起大憂慮：勿我財寶當為王賊之所侵奪，或火焚燒，或水漂蕩，或宿惡作當令滅壞，或現非理作業方便當令散失，
items.en: Because of this, one must wash daily — should a hand, a foot, or any other limb accidentally touch [waste], both oneself and others feel revulsion. This same cause also gives rise to manifold illness within the body. …Such countless illnesses arise in the body because of food. Or, because what was eaten was poorly balanced, it remains undigested within the body. This is called the fault of transformation in food. …It is like one who, for the sake of food, is afflicted by cold in cold weather and afflicted by heat in hot weather, exerting oneself and toiling with great hardship. …Having toiled and exerted oneself in this way, seeking food, should the undertaking not succeed, one becomes sorrowful, anxious, and distressed, beating one's chest and lamenting, weeping and despondent: "Why has all my effort come to nothing?" …Should the undertaking succeed, one then gives rise, in order to protect it, to great anxiety: may my wealth not be seized by kings or bandits, not burned by fire, not swept away by flood, not ruined by some past unwholesome deed, not dissipated through some present unwise transaction...

items.zh: 或諸非愛、或宿共財當所理奪，或即家中當生家火，由是當令財寶虧損。如是名為於食防護所作過患。云何於食能壞親愛所作過患？
items.en: or that it may be seized through legal claims by those who bear me ill will or by those with whom I formerly shared the property, or that a fire may break out in my own house — and so my wealth would be diminished. This is called the fault of food arising from guarding it. What is called the fault of food that destroys affection?

items.title: Section: From Broken Families to War Itself — The Pursuit's Final Faults, and a Deathbed Vision of Encroaching Dark

items.zh: 謂諸世間，為食因緣多起鬪諍。父子、母女、兄弟、朋友尚為飲食互相非毀，況非親里為食因緣而不展轉更相鬪訟。所謂大族諸婆羅門、剎帝利種、長者、居士，為食因緣迭興違諍，以其手足塊刀杖等互相加害。是名於食能壞親愛所作過患。云何於食無有厭足所作過患？謂諸國王剎帝利種，位登灌頂，亦於自國王都聚落不住喜足，俱帥兵戈，互相征討。吹以貝角，扣擊鍾鼓，揮刀、槃矟、放箭、𥎞矛，車馬象步交橫馳亂；種種戈仗傷害其身，或便致死，或等死苦。復有所餘如是等類。是名於食無有厭足所作過患。云何因食不得自在所作過患？謂如一類，為王所使，討固牢城，因遭種種極熱脂油、熱牛糞汁及鎔銅鐵而相注灑，或被戈杖、傷害其身，或便致死，或等死苦。復有所餘如是等類。是名因食不得自在所作過患。云何因食起諸惡行所作過患？謂如有一，為食因緣，造作積集身諸惡行。如身惡行，語、意亦爾。臨命終時，為諸重病苦所逼切。由先所作諸身語意種種惡行增上力故，於日後分，見有諸山、或諸山峯垂影懸覆、近覆、極覆。便作是念：我自昔來依身語意所造諸業，唯罪非福。若有其趣，諸造惡者當生其中，我今定往。如是悔已，尋即捨命。既捨命已，隨業差別生諸惡趣。謂那洛迦、傍生、餓鬼。
items.en: In the world, disputes over food frequently arise: even fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, brothers, and friends slander one another over food — how much more so those who are not kin at all. …[Great families] harm one another with their hands, feet, stones, knives, and clubs. This is called the fault of destroying affection. …Kings of the warrior caste, having ascended the throne, remain unsatisfied even with their own kingdoms, cities, and villages, and lead their armies to wage war against one another … wounding one another's bodies with every kind of weapon, sometimes to death, sometimes to a suffering equal to death. This is called the fault of insatiability. …It is like one sent by a king to besiege a fortified city, who then suffers scalding oil, boiling dung, or molten copper and iron poured down upon them, or is wounded by weapons, sometimes to death, sometimes to a suffering equal to death. This is called the fault of losing one's freedom because of food. …It is like one who, for the sake of food, commits and accumulates bodily misconduct — and just as with bodily misconduct, so too with verbal and mental misconduct. …At the time of death, oppressed by the pain of grave illness, through the power of the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct previously committed, one sees, as at the sun's late afternoon, the shadows of mountains or mountain peaks beginning to fall — first partially covering, then drawing nearer, then covering everything entirely. One then thinks: "Everything I have done through body, speech, and mind, from long ago until now, has been nothing but wrongdoing, never merit. If such destinations exist, all who have done wrong are destined for them — I too shall surely go there now." Having thought this with regret, one's life then comes to an end. Having died, one is reborn, according to the particular nature of one's karma, into one of the unfortunate realms — hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

items.zh: 如是名為因食惡行所作過患。如是段食，於追求時有諸過患，於受用時有諸過患，於轉變時有諸過患。
items.en: This is called the fault of food arising from misconduct committed on account of food. Thus this solid food has faults at the time it is sought, faults at the time it is consumed, and faults at the time it is transformed [in the body].

blocks.text: The faults of food continue, now widening from the body to society. The passage ends with an image of dying.
Food requires daily washing, brings many illnesses, and, poorly balanced, stays undigested. Master Cháng Bǎi: "illness enters by the mouth."

"For the sake of food, one is afflicted by cold in cold weather and by heat in hot weather, exerting oneself with great hardship." Sometimes the effort fails entirely. Master Cháng Bǎi: people say no effort is wasted, but here it is. Unwise dealings in this life, "misjudging people, buying the wrong stocks", also count.

Even fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, brothers and friends slander one another over food. Kings, even those consecrated with water from the four oceans, go to war for it. One who serves a king loses one's freedom: "one cannot say 'I won't go'." Master Cháng Bǎi quotes the saying: people die for wealth as birds die for food.

Those who did wrong to obtain food see, at death, a darkness like a mountain's shadow in the evening: first "hanging over", then "drawing near", then "completely covering". Master Cháng Bǎi explains the three stages. Venerable Miào Jìng: those with evil karma go from light into darkness at death.

The chain from a meal to a war seems exaggerated until one thinks of how much of the world's conflict is, in the end, about resources. The treatise asks the meditator to see that chain before sitting down to eat.

quiz.q: The text says countless illnesses arise because of food. What common saying does Master Cháng Bǎi cite?
options: three meals a day
early to bed, early to rise
hardship is nourishment
illness enters by the mouth — improper eating brings on all kinds of disease
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: people say illness enters by the mouth — because improper eating gives rise to every sort of disease.

quiz.q: How does the treatise describe the hardship of pursuing food?
options: simply waiting for it to be brought
hardship only in summer
afflicted by cold in cold weather and by heat in hot weather, toiling with great hardship
only the poor suffer
quiz.why: "It is like one who, for the sake of food, is afflicted by cold in cold weather and afflicted by heat in hot weather, exerting oneself and toiling with great hardship." Master Cháng Bǎi: to get food or amass wealth, every trade must endure cold and heat.

quiz.q: When the venture fails, one laments that the effort was in vain. What saying does Master Cháng Bǎi contrast this with?
options: people say "no effort is wasted," yet here the effort is wasted
where there's a will there's a way
there's no free lunch
failure is the mother of success
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: why work so hard and earn nothing? People say no effort is wasted, but here the effort is wasted without result.

quiz.q: The text says disputes over food arise often — even among whom? What saying does Master Cháng Bǎi cite?
options: only strangers; "a near neighbour beats a distant relative"
only enemy states; "know yourself and your enemy"
fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, brothers, friends; "people die for wealth, birds for food"
only monastics; "a day without work, a day without food"
quiz.why: Even fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, brothers, and friends slander one another over food. Master Cháng Bǎi: as the saying goes, people die for wealth and birds for food — this is the third fault of pursuit, destroying affection.

quiz.q: The text speaks of kings "consecrated" on the throne. What does Venerable Miào Jìng say the consecration is?
options: anointing with oil
receiving bodhisattva precepts
being crowned
the rite in which the supreme ruler, on taking office, is sprinkled with water of the four great oceans
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: it is the ceremony in which the person of highest power, on taking office, is sprinkled with water from the four great oceans. Even such a one is not content and leads armies against others.

quiz.q: Being sent by a king to besiege a city and suffering scalding oil and molten metal is called what fault?
options: destroying affection
losing one's freedom because of food
consumption
transformation
quiz.why: "This is called the fault of losing one's freedom because of food." Venerable Miào Jìng: under the king's orders one is not free — one cannot say "I won't go to war."

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain the three stages of the mountain shadow at death?
options: they all mean the same
three different mountains
three nights
partial covering, the darkness drawing nearer, and finally total darkness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: hanging cover is a small part darkened by shadow; near cover, the darkness approaches and the mountain seems almost covered; extreme cover, complete darkness at last.
